_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for San Marino covering Saint Marinus founding (~301 CE, Christian stonemason fled Diocletian persecution, Mount Titano), medieval commune, independence maintained (not conquered by Italy, Napoleon respected it), neutrality in both World Wars, modern tourism economy, and oldest republic continuously in existence.

country_profile.currency: Euro (EUR) (mints own coins by agreement with EU)

religion.note: Roman Catholic (not state religion in constitution but deeply embedded); founding legend of Saint Marinus (Christian stonemason, 301 CE, Mount Titano hermit, built chapel, community formed); Basilica di San Marino; Catholic patrimony but modern separation of church and state

ethnic_groups.name: Sammarinese
ethnic_groups.notes: Citizens (citizenship difficult to obtain, based on descent or 30 years residence + naturalization); Italian-speaking; tiny nation (33k people, everyone knows everyone); strong local identity despite Italian culture

ethnic_groups.name: Italian
ethnic_groups.notes: Resident foreigners; workers; cultural unity with Italy (language, customs)

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Romanian, Ukrainian, Filipino; small immigrant workforce

independence.from: Legendary founding by Saint Marinus (301 CE); independence maintained continuously; world's oldest republic

country_profile.notes_unique: Oldest republic in world (founded 301 CE, oldest continuously surviving sovereign state and constitutional republic, 1,700+ years); third-smallest European state (after Vatican, Monaco); enclaved entirely within Italy (Mount Titano, 749m peak); unique diarchy (two Captains Regent, Capitani Reggenti, serve 6 months, elected twice/year April+October since 1243, ensures no single ruler); Napoleon respected independence (1797 offered to expand territory, San Marino declined); never conquered; avoided Italian unification (Garibaldi took refuge 1849, grateful, respected independence 1861); neutral in both World Wars (WWII: sheltered 100k refugees, bombed once by RAF by mistake); no debt (balanced budget constitutionally required); ceramic/tourism economy; postage stamps (collectors); oldest written constitution still in effect (1600, Leges Statutae Republicae Sanct Marini); nine municipalities (castelli); three towers on Mount Titano (Guaita/Cesta/Montale, national symbols, on flag/coat of arms); UNESCO World Heritage Site

current_leader.name: Two Captains Regent (rotated every 6 months)
current_leader.title: Captains Regent (Capitani Reggenti)
current_leader.notes: Diarchy unique system; two co-equal heads of state serve 6-month terms; elected by Grand and General Council; ceremonial and symbolic but represent continuity since 1243; current pair (as of Apr-Oct 2025 term): Francesca Civerchia and Dalibor Riccardi; ensures no single autocrat

former_leaders.name: Various Captains Regent
former_leaders.notes: 1,600+ pairs of Captains Regent over 780+ years; notable recent pairs include first female Captain Regent Maria Lea Pedini-Angelini (1981); system prevented dictatorship; symbol of republican continuity

910.name: Foundation by Saint Marinus
910.description: According to tradition, Saint Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab, founded a monastic community atop Monte Titano in 301 CE, fleeing Emperor Diocletian's persecution. This legendary foundation makes San Marino the world's oldest surviving republic.

sub_clusters.name: Saint Marinus & the Monte Titano Community
sub_clusters.description: The legendary founding of a Christian hermit community on Monte Titano by Saint Marinus (301 CE), the formation of a self-governing commune, and its survival through the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
key_events: Saint Marinus founds a community on Monte Titano (traditional date: 3 Sept 301)

920.name: Medieval Commune & Independence
920.description: San Marino evolved from a monastic community into a self-governing commune. By the 13th century it had established the Captains Regent system and secured papal recognition of its independence, navigating the complex politics of the Italian peninsula.

sub_clusters.name: Commune Formation & Early Statutes
sub_clusters.description: The gradual development of communal self-governance, the early statutes, and the establishment of the Arengo (assembly of heads of families) as the governing body.

sub_clusters.name: Captains Regent & Papal Recognition
sub_clusters.description: The institution of the two Captains Regent (1263) serving six-month terms—a system still in use today—and papal recognition of San Marino's liberty, plus territorial expansion to its current borders.
key_events: Institution of the dual Captains Regent system (1263)
Pope Nicholas IV recognises San Marino's independence (1291)

930.name: Renaissance & Early Modern Survival
930.description: San Marino survived the turbulent era of Cesare Borgia, the wars of Italian city-states, and the consolidation of the Papal States by maintaining strict neutrality and leveraging its mountainous terrain and diplomatic skill.

sub_clusters.name: Borgia Threat & Malatesta Wars
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's defiance of Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta's aggression, Cesare Borgia's brief occupation (1503), and the republic's recovery and reaffirmation of independence.

sub_clusters.name: Early Modern Neutrality & Papal Relations
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's delicate diplomacy with the Papal States, the failed Cardinal Alberoni occupation (1739–40), and the republic's continued survival through strict neutrality.
key_events: Cardinal Alberoni's occupation of San Marino foiled; independence restored (1740)

930.name: Napoleonic Encounter
930.description: Napoleon Bonaparte, respecting San Marino's republican tradition, not only spared the tiny state but offered to extend its territory and provide supplies—an offer the Sammarinese wisely declined to avoid entanglements.

sub_clusters.name: Napoleon & the Offer of Territory
sub_clusters.description: Napoleon's recognition of and respect for San Marino during his Italian campaigns, the offer of territorial expansion and grain, and the republic's prudent refusal.
key_events: Napoleon offers San Marino expanded territory; the republic declines (1797)

940.name: Italian Unification & Neutrality
940.description: During the Risorgimento, San Marino sheltered Italian patriots including Giuseppe Garibaldi. When Italy unified, San Marino negotiated a treaty of friendship (1862) that preserved its independence while all other Italian microstates were absorbed.

sub_clusters.name: Shelter for Garibaldi & Italian Patriots
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's role as a refuge for Italian patriots during the Risorgimento, most famously sheltering Giuseppe Garibaldi and 2,000 followers fleeing Austrian and papal forces in 1849.
key_events: Garibaldi and 2,000 followers take refuge in San Marino (1849)

sub_clusters.name: Treaty of Friendship with Italy
sub_clusters.description: The 1862 treaty with the Kingdom of Italy guaranteeing San Marino's sovereignty, modernisation efforts including railway and postal services, and the republic's unique survival amid Italian nation-building.

950.name: World Wars & Neutrality
950.description: San Marino declared neutrality in both World Wars but was accidentally bombed by the RAF in 1944 and briefly occupied by German and then Allied forces. Post-war, San Marino briefly had a communist government—unique in Western Europe.

sub_clusters.name: WWI Neutrality & Limited Involvement
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's declared neutrality in World War I, though it provided a small volunteer corps and a field hospital to the Italian war effort.

sub_clusters.name: WWII – RAF Bombing & Occupation
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's declaration of neutrality, the influx of over 100,000 refugees, the accidental RAF bombing (26 June 1944) killing 63 civilians, and brief German then Allied occupation.
key_events: RAF accidentally bombs neutral San Marino, killing 63 (26 June 1944)

sub_clusters.name: Post-War Communist Government
sub_clusters.description: San Marino's unique communist-socialist coalition government (1945–57), one of the only communist governments in Western Europe elected democratically, and the 1957 'Fatti di Rovereta' crisis that ended it.

960.name: Modern Microstate & European Integration
960.description: San Marino modernised its economy, joined the Council of Europe and the UN, adopted the euro through agreement with the EU, and maintained its ancient republican institutions while becoming a modern European microstate.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Consolidation & UN Membership
sub_clusters.description: Political stabilisation after the communist era, women's suffrage (1964), UN membership (1992), and the modernisation of San Marino's legal and political systems.
key_events: San Marino grants women the right to vote (1964)
San Marino joins the United Nations (2 March 1992)

sub_clusters.name: Euro Adoption & Tourism Economy
sub_clusters.description: Customs union with the EU, adoption of the euro (2002) via monetary agreement, the economy's shift from philately and tourism to finance, and ongoing negotiations for closer EU association.
